What’s !important #19: CSS Refraction Effects, Scroll State Queries, @custom-media, and More

📅 2026-10-27  |  Read Source →

We’re back! Don’t worry, this isn’t a trick (despite what our name suggests!). However, due to the hiatus, we’re also a little behind. That’s why this issue of What’s !important is absolutely stacked. All killer, no filler. Here’s what you missed.

By the way, before we dive in, Mat Marquis’ highly recommended JavaScript for Everyone course is currently -30% off (code: CSSTRICKSFRIENDS). You don’t want to miss this.

Preethi Sam demonstrated how to create background image refraction effects with CSS. The effects are stunning, can be animated, don’t need very much CSS (no JavaScript), and we don’t need to duplicate the image either.

Brecht De Ruyte demonstrated how to build customizable components using container style queries and advanced attr(), showcasing some incredible interactive demos, including the two below:

Dan Holloran showed us how to use the different scroll-state() queries (scrollable, scrolled, snapped, and stuck). It’s not a long read, which is exactly what you want for a new but simple feature like this.

A quick, no-context CSS snippet to entice you:

Declan Chidlow shared some of the craziest CSS to ever exist, and I mean craziest. Most of it comes from Internet Explorer, but let’s face it, you knew that already. Thankfully, they don’t build them like they used to.

Bramus demonstrated how to animate CSS grids using anchor positioning. The idea is that we anchor content to its corresponding cell, and then as the grid reflows, it’s the content (not the cell) that animates with it.

(But it doesn’t work in Firefox due to what sounds like a bug.)

Chris Coyier talked about a bunch of new HTML features, and honestly, there’s a whole lot in there that you definitely haven’t heard of. Like, I’m certain of it.

Victor Ayomipo contemplated why container query adoption has been so terrible despite them topping CSS wishlists for years. Victor thinks that we’re using them wrong, so he’s here to set the record straight.

Cory LaViska demonstrated how to use @custom-media in addition to container style queries as a fallback.

Also, don’t forget that Declan has an extremely thorough @custom-media deep-dive in our Almanac.

Ahmad Shadeed tackled an interesting topic — detecting overlapping elements (with CSS, of course). If you’re keen on anchor positioning, scroll-driven animations, and again (!), container style queries, then this walkthrough is for you.

I want to know when the decorative element hits the section from the left edge, taking into consideration that the element might have a fluid position or size that changes with the viewport size or container size. Basically, it’s a dynamic problem. It’s not about using a media query to hide the decorative element, I want to hide it upon overlapping.

Maybe container queries are finally picking up?

Patrick Brosset walked us through a proposal for the previewsrc HTML attribute, which would enable us to supply preview images for images that haven’t yet loaded using only HTML. For example, we could supply a blurry preview image. However, I’d rather have something like :loaded/:not(:loaded) so that we can style/transition unloaded images with CSS rather than needing to create extra images.

Temani Afif shared a custom borders demo, where the trick is to declare a transparent border, use border-shape to define its shape, then declare a background in addition to background-clip: border-area so that it only shows up within the border, like this (requires Chrome at the moment):

In a similar manner, Leon Arnott shared this awesome trick for animating the background color of ::selection, something that’s actually forbidden (or so we thought, anyway…):

Today in CSS: We all know you can change the highlight colour of selected text, but it's impossible to animate that colour. Unless… the colour was just a variable inherited from the parent element, using @​property to make it animatable… Hahahahaha… [image or embed]

And that’s it, really. Simply use var(--bg-color) on ::selection or some other visually restrictive element.

Chris Coyier demonstrated how to random()ly animate an element along the edge of another element. There’s a cute doggo, by the way. Probably should’ve led with that.

Polypane explained how we might disable the root scroller accidentally (which is surprisingly easy to do — I’ve definitely done it), what we lose in doing so, and what to do instead.

Also, have you ever completely misunderstood how the root (:root/html) works? This is a solid explainer for that, too.

Speaking of accidents, have you ever tapped on a target twice, apparently in quick succession, and ended up zooming in? Andy Bell revealed that touch-action: manipulation disables the double-tap-to-zoom-in functionality. It isn’t new, but I don’t see many web developers using it. One for the CSS reset, I think?

Chrome and Firefox now ship every two weeks. The inaugural releases were fairly exciting (not smaller, as I assumed they’d be). In addition, Safari 27 (along with iOS, iPadOS, and macOS 27) shipped with some of the same features as Firefox, making them Baseline in the same release window. High fives all around!

The Nightmare Before Retirement: A Physician’s Cautionary Tale (2026 Edition)

📅 2026-10-27  |  Read Source →

“I’m sick of the scaring, the terror, the fright. I’m tired of being something that goes bump in the night. I’m bored with leering my horrible glances, And my feet hurt from dancing those skeleton dances. I don’t like graveyards, and I need something new. There must be more to life than just yelling, ‘Boo!'”

—Tim Burton, The Nightmare Before Christmas

Dr. Wednesday Addams sat alone in her office at 11 PM, glaring at her retirement calculator the way you’d glare at a pathology report you already suspect is bad.

Twenty years of serious income, the kind that makes the neighbors assume you’re rich, and the screen looked like a crime scene.

Projected retirement age: 79. Probability of success: 23%. Her portfolio had roughly the life expectancy of a jack-o’-lantern left on the porch until Thanksgiving.

She was 58. She wanted out at 61, and blocking the exit stood a tangle of whole life policies her cousin had sold her, a 401(k) ignored for a decade, a pre-tax balance quietly wiring itself into a tax bomb, and a household burning $35,000 a month like a furnace nobody remembered to turn down.

Her story isn’t rare. It isn’t even interesting.

Physicians stumble into the same open graves with the reliability of a zombie shuffling toward the nearest brain, and the tax code waiting at the bottom helps itself to 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700. Some of these graves are fresh. A few were dug by Congress.

The AMA’s latest national data has 41.9% of physicians reporting at least one symptom of burnout in 2025, down from 48.2% in 2023. Progress, technically. Emergency medicine and hematology-oncology still sit near 50%, coin-flip odds that the physician running tonight’s code is cooked.

Burnout steals your joy first and your retirement date second. You plan to work until 68, the call schedule wins at 61, and the seven years of full income your plan quietly assumed shrink to a few years of part-time pay, or nothing at all.

The itch is arriving earlier, too. In Doximity’s polling, the share of physicians aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, from 23% to 44%.

Dr. Smart and Dr. Addams both started at 35 earning $300,000. Smart saved 25%, or $75,000 a year. Addams saved 10%.

Run that $45,000 annual gap through 25 years at a 5% real return and it grows to about $2.15 million by age 60, a fortune separating two doctors with the same income at the same hospital, parked in the same doctors’ lot, one of them driving home to a plan and the other to a calculator that reads like a death certificate.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Addams spent every productivity bonus. You’ve already met her at 11 PM.

You go from a resident making $65,000 to an attending earning $350,000, and the word “deserve” moves into your vocabulary. A bigger house. Then tens of thousands sunk into renovating it, followed by the new car, the au pair, private school, and first class to Maui.

Nobody warns you how hard it is to downshift once you’ve gotten used to the view. Your brain resets “normal” to match your paycheck and refuses to reset it back, so the spending tags along into retirement like a party guest who showed up uninvited and also brought luggage.

I watched an Arizona cardiologist discover at 66 that he needed $400,000 a year to keep living the way he lived. His portfolio could safely throw off maybe $180,000. He’s 71 now. Still full-time.

Simple, boring solution: live like a resident for two to five years after training, bank the gap, kill the student loans, and upgrade slowly enough that your brain never registers the drift.

Nearly every physician gets pitched whole life insurance, usually by a friend or relative whose licensing exam ink is still wet. The illustration promises cash value, tax-free growth, and a death benefit, all in one tidy package.

For most physicians who need life insurance, it’s mostly garbage. Premiums run many times higher than term. Commissions feed on the early years, and the cash value grows like it’s been bled.

Run an illustrative comparison: one physician pays $3,000 a month into whole life, while her colleague buys 20-year term for around $150 a month and invests the other $2,850, and at a 7% return that side account sits near $1.5 million after 20 years, with the policy’s cash value usually trailing by hundreds of thousands, still waiting for the illustration to come true.

Sold by family, illustrated in optimistic colors, and funded for 15 years by a doctor too busy to read past page two, Dr. Addams’s three policies carried combined premiums of $8,400 a month and a total cash value of $780,000.

Term plus investing would likely have left her near $1.9 million. She surrendered all three at 58. Ate the surrender charges. Started catching up.

In plenty of physician households, one person earns the money and the same person manages it.

Then the doctor dies, divorces, or has a stroke at 63, and the spouse inherits decades of decisions made behind a closed door, written in a language nobody bothered to teach them.

I’ve sat with widows who found out their physician husband had:

A spouse at the table pulls decisions toward the conservative side, a handy counterweight when the 2 AM version of you thinks genius has struck.

Build the plan simple enough that they could run it alone. Keep the account list and passwords somewhere they can actually find, which rules out your head.

Business school professors have a phrase for the bad investments that circulate in medical circles: deals that can only be sold to doctors.

Time poverty and overconfidence do the damage. Researching an investment takes hours you don’t have, so you trust people, and you assume that mastering the coagulation cascade somehow qualifies you to underwrite private equity. It doesn’t.

Physicians I know have poured money into restaurant groups that folded within 18 months, real estate “opportunities” that smelled faintly of Ponzi, and crypto tokens launched by a nephew’s roommate’s brother.

Index funds are boring. They work. Put $50,000 a year into low-cost index funds for 30 years at a 5% real return and you end up with about $3.32 million.

Lose 2% a year to fees and the same contributions grow to about $2.38 million, close to a million dollars handed to people in nicer suits than yours. If your portfolio needs a 40-page binder to explain, you’re the mark.

Most physicians blow past the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December, which puts you among the few groups who routinely qualify for the maximum benefit. Claiming age is a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month. Wait until full retirement age and that rises to $4,152. Hold out to 70 and it’s roughly $5,181.

Dr. Lucky filed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums at $200 an hour, and because Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 before full retirement age, his own paycheck ate his benefit, which the SSA hands back after full retirement age in small monthly crumbs.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a premium no insurer will match. A serious diagnosis can justify claiming early.

For a healthy 62-year-old with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call. You’ve delivered enough prognoses to know which patient you are.

Most physicians stuff nearly everything into pre-tax accounts during peak years, which makes sense at 37%. Trouble arrives when that’s the only move for 25 years, because a $4 million pre-tax portfolio is a smaller number dressed up for the party.

If you need $180,000 a year to live and pull it entirely from pre-tax accounts, you might withdraw $240,000 to get there. Your 4.5% withdrawal plan just became a 6% plan.

Required minimum distributions start at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security. Then Medicare notices.

IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at modified AGI of $218,000 for married couples, and at the top tier Part B jumps from $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, roughly $6,900 a year per person, a fine levied for the crime of saving diligently in the wrong bucket.

Medicare looks back two years, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

But if you retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade of taxable income lower than anything since residency, a window for converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth on purpose, in measured doses, the way you’d titrate a drip rather than push a bolus.

While you’re still working, fund a backdoor Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan. If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already decided for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions go in as Roth.

Asset location matters too, and municipal bonds can help outside retirement accounts.

At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, close to 41 cents of every taxable bond interest dollar goes to Washington. Keep bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b). Hold broad stock index funds in taxable.

Two physicians can retire with identical portfolios and identical withdrawal rates and still get completely different endings. Timing decides which. Finance calls it sequence of returns risk, and you’ll call it something less printable.

Retire in February 2020 and you watched the Dow fall from about 29,550 to under 19,000 in roughly six weeks. Retire into 2022 and the S&P 500 dropped about 19% as inflation spiked.

Even 2025 had teeth: the S&P 500 fell almost 19% between its February high and early April as tariff headlines rattled markets.

Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (whose name keeps aging badly) retires into a bear market, sells near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back.

William Bengen’s 4% rule, published in 1994, tries to account for that, and Bengen has since nudged his own number up to about 4.7%. The real mistake is treating any figure as carved on a tombstone.

Retirees who trim spending after bad years, or who keep two to five years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds, give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Dr. Addams checked her allocation at 59 and found 95% stocks, 5% cash, and no plan for a crash. She moved to 60/30/10 stocks, bonds, and cash and started building a three-year buffer. Her mix won’t fit everyone, but “I’ll figure it out when it happens” fits nobody.

Don’t overcorrect into a bond basement either. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years, so stocks still have work to do.

CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Inflation cooled. Prices didn’t.

A $200,000 retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation, and any income stream that doesn’t adjust, whether a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, or a practice buyout paid in level installments, shrinks every year you hold it, rotting quietly from the inside the way pumpkins do.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician pay has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 after adjusting for practice-cost inflation.

Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched eat your fee schedule.

Your brother needs $50,000 for a business. Your sister needs $30,000 to stop a foreclosure.

A few years later your kid asks for $80,000 toward a house, because you’re the rich doctor, and the rich doctor is who people call, and nobody in the history of families has ever called the rich doctor to pay him back.

Treat money to family as a gift with no strings, sized to what you can afford to never see again. Dr. Addams lent her brother $120,000 for a restaurant. It failed. He filed for bankruptcy, and they haven’t spoken in six years.

Long-term rental losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income. Short-term rentals play by different rules.

If the average guest stay runs seven days or less and you materially participate, most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more than any other individual, the losses turn non-passive and can offset W-2 or 1099 income (a separate route from Real Estate Professional Status), the closest thing the tax code offers to a garlic necklace for your paycheck.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently restored for property acquired after January 19, 2025.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, worth roughly $55,000 to $74,000 in federal tax at 37%.

Locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work: if any of it lands on a 1099, a Solo 401(k) usually beats the SEP-IRA most contractors open by default. For 2026 you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (shared with any W-2 plan you also use), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings, up to $72,000 combined, with $8,000 in catch-up at 50 or $11,250 between 60 and 63. The SEP also poisons your backdoor Roth through the pro-rata rule.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan on top, where contributions often reach six figures for doctors in their 50s. Those deductions pull double duty because of the QBI cliff.

For 2026, married couples get the full 20% qualified business income deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it disappears at $553,500. A married 1099 doc with $500,000 of taxable income who funds both plans can slide below $403,500 and watch the deduction rise from the dead.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger one, and a market dip talks you into another year, then another, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve considered slowing down.

Every year worked past enough gets paid for with a year you’ll never get back at that age, a year of knees that still handle a trail and a back that still lifts a grandkid, traded for a margin of safety your spreadsheet stopped needing long ago, which makes one more year the only prescription in medicine with no ceiling dose.

Physicians who bolt without a plan for Monday get haunted by the opposite problem. You were Dr. Johnson, the cardiologist. Now you’re Bob, with 50 empty hours a week and no idea what to put in them.

Some Bobs end up unretiring just to have somewhere to be.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Easing out tends to go better than slamming the door. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or teaching keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow untouched a few more years.

Watch for a malpractice tail bill on a claims-made policy, and remember that governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age.

In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those simply running from the pager.

Dr. Addams caught her mistakes at 58 instead of 68, and that gave her room to work. She hired a fee-only fiduciary advisor, wrote a plan, surrendered the bad policies, sold the vacation home, and maxed every account she had.

She retired at 64 on about $18,000 a month instead of $35,000. Plenty, it turned out.

Several year-end moves for 2026 can’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

For the rest of the year, check every beneficiary form, add up 12 months of actual spending, swap whole life for adequate term and disability coverage where it makes sense, and bring your spouse into the conversation. Then raise your savings rate 1 to 2 points every year until you hit 25% to 30% of gross.

You’ll make mistakes. Everyone does. What matters is catching them at 58, the way Dr. Addams did, while the options are still standing in the room, instead of at 70, when most of them have left the building and switched off the porch light behind them.

Pick one item from this list before the first trick-or-treater rings your doorbell. Make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

I’ve made some of these mistakes in my 30s by falling into the luxury trap when decent salaries first hit the accounts. Living in Los Angeles it would be VERY easy to burn 35k per month without luxury cars or private schools. In fact we’re not too far off and we drive older EV cars that are paid off and the kids go to great public schools. The costs of living have increased to the point of needing to pay very close attention to all expenses and max out investment and retirement accounts even when it hurts. We’ve started catching rounding 40, traveling a bit less, no new cars, only making required fixes to the house. After reading this I’m more confident that we’ve made the right decisions to get smart and aggressive about this now.

Interesting article focused on finances with a smattering of other issues. Importantly, what are your support systems upon retirement, like spouse, friends, etc.? Sometimes friends are not there because they choose to move closer to their children or they are deceased. What are your interests in medicine and outside medicine? What are your hobbies? Do you want to volunteer? You have been going 90 miles mph and then slow down to 10 mph. Without some kind of plan to fill your time, with and without your spouse/significant other, this is a recipe for depression and disaster. Do you want to stay connected to medicine in some way? Maybe you can observe trainees doing an H&P and counseling. Maybe you can offer advice as to how to set up an office practice for senior residents. In another ote, how is your health and do you take care of yourself? Going into retirement with significant health issues can influence how your retirement goes and when you retire, perhaps restricting travel and other activities. We have written an article on retirement that might compliment the informative blog here. Whereas it is focused on academic physicians, there are many points applicable to those in practice (Greenberg L, Fischel JE, Siegel B. Academic clinician educators: Confronting the challenges to successful retirement. Educ Health (Abingdon). 2023 Jan-Apr;36(1):24-32. doi: 10.4103/efh.efh_192_22. PMID: 38047344.). Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

I am so sorry, you lost me at the fact that you actually were burning 35k per month!!! how is that even possible!!! you are exactly where you chose to be, its consequences. Most of us, and I honestly believe I speak for the majority of physicians, do not even get remotely close to such an exaggerated figure. Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

They left out the annuity with a 5% rate guaranteed growth with step ups if the market does better than 5% minus fees. You can attach an ins package for your spouse. take a 4% W/D on your money. dont increase your standard of living to just be like everyone else. avoid the race to nowhere and stay away from out of state tuition. your kids will do well anywhere they go if they apply themselves: they got the intellect and drive from their parents not private school or private universities. Cars get you to and from work – where is the luxury? in the car dealerships pocket. The Power of Loving Awareness

📅 2026-10-26  |  Read Source →

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Mindfulness can’t always change the outcome when life gets hard, but showing up with loving awareness can ease suffering and deepen our connection to each other.

Life is hard, and it might get harder. So, where could mindfulness or loving awareness fit in when survival feels tenuous and ultimately temporary?

Recently, I listened to a good friend sharing painful accounts of his health crisis, the loss of his sister to cancer, and how his work is suffering as a result. It all sounded pretty grim. I could sense his anxiety and distress, so I told him that sometimes I cheer myself up with this image: It’s like we’re on the Titanic and we’re all going down, but it’s ok because we have our arms around each other as we sink into the ocean.

After a moment of stunned silence, my friend said, “Is that your idea of comforting me?”

After a moment of stunned silence, my friend said, “Is that your idea of comforting me? That we’re on the Titanic as it’s sinking!!?” And then, because he knows I practice mindfulness, he added: “Is this your idea of mindfulness?”

I paused to reflect for a moment and replied, “Well, I guess I’m being mindful that this is my thought, and that by acknowledging it I can gently and kindly be present to whatever it brings up. Besides, I’m focusing on the part that we all have our arms around each other.”

I mean, c’mon. Yes, there is so much unhinging crap that we have to wade through every day. And most of us have very little control over important things that affect our safety and well-being, so it makes sense that uncertainty brings up worry and anxiety.

So, how could mindfulness hope to solve this? Good question!

For decades, all my plans to drink more water, practice the piano, and regularly go to the gym never seemed to gain traction. But I’ve kept returning to a mindfulness practice, even though it can be irritating to become more aware, like when I realize I’m judging, or that I just want to keep judging or gossiping, or stay impatient or demanding. It’s easier, often, just to carry on with the slime.

It can be irritating to become more aware, like when I realize I’m judging, or that I just want to keep judging or gossiping, or stay impatient or demanding.

But then, much to the chagrin of that part of me that just wants to scream into people’s faces, years of practicing mindfulness cause me to stop and look at whatever strong thoughts and emotions I’m laying myself open to and ask this question: “Will leaning into hate and divisiveness take me closer to, or further from, who I really want to be?”

Not to mention that rage-venting also does NOT make those bad feelings go away. Actually, it usually makes them worse. The ragey-ness supports a dark narrative, blocks nourishing positive interactions, and cuts me off from more complicated emotions, the ones I could see, welcome, and learn from if I had enough calm and presence.

So, a mindfulness question: What meaning arises when we show up with loving awareness…no matter what’s happening?

My mother lies dying in front of me. There are no words left to exchange. I hold her hand quietly for hour upon hour. She does not appear to be conscious, but I figure, you never know. I hold her close, no cell phone scrolling, just loving presence. I hope this might help her feel that she is safe and surrounded by caring love…wherever she is.

I have a thought: I am ferrying her from this side to the other. And I don’t want her to be afraid, since nothing can stop her from going.

I have a thought: I am ferrying her from this side to the other. And I don’t want her to be afraid, since nothing can stop her from going. Every once in a while, I tell her that everything is OK, and that she can go anytime she needs to.

At the end, at her end, there was nothing to do. There was only loving awareness. “Hello, Mom. Fran. Frances. You’re not alone. Do you feel my hand? Love is here with you. And, we are taking that ferry together, as far as I am allowed to go.”

I could not stop my mother from dying. Not only that, I’ve not been able to stop the climate crisis, or prevent so much gut-wrenching harm.

Mindfulness might not change an outcome, but it can reduce suffering by increasing loving connection.

Sometimes loving awareness might mean finding your voice, or your courage, and taking action against harms. Sometimes it might come down to bravely bearing witness to others’ suffering. Mindfulness might not change an outcome, but it can reduce suffering by increasing loving connection.

In fact, in my experience, that is a superpower.

You might meet people who practice mindfulness and still aren’t very nice. Well, mindfulness isn’t necessarily going to immediately make any of us a nicer or more loving or less judgy person. That requires choosing to take the actions that loving awareness illuminates, over and over again.

Practicing mindfulness can help us step back and hold ourselves in loving awareness before we lose our cool. And by using a mindful approach, we can learn to break habits like viewing everything and everyone as the enemy. We can learn how to intentionally engage with our vagus nerve to help regulate the body’s stress response. It can be as ordinary as extending your out-breath, a simple technique for helping the body stabilize.

When we are already feeling rocky, automatic thoughts and fears often trigger a threat response, appropriate when there’s danger to escape from. But without mindful awareness, we risk remaining caught in that response long after it’s helpful. When we get stuck in a dark narrative, when we don’t accept the invitation that loving awareness offers us, we can end up unintentionally zapping ourselves with adrenaline and cortisol, amping up our stress over and over, which you may have noticed is very depleting.

When we practice loving awareness, we are inviting ourselves to notice whatever shows up, without judgment. This might include how unpleasant it can feel to sit in so-called silence. At first, we might be overwhelmed by the busy buzzing blender of thoughts going on in our heads. You can picture your thoughts as grains of sand in a jar of muddy water. Shake the jar up and notice how long it takes for all the grains to settle. So, a few minutes of focused meditation might help some of your thoughts settle. But there are so many! That means you might not notice much difference at first.

Practice includes noticing what you’ve been ignoring, like unpleasant sensations of tightness and tension in your body, or difficult emotions you’ve spent years suppressing.

There are a million ways to practice mindfulness. For instance, you might try hugging yourself, or placing a kind hand on your cheek or forehead or belly. When you do, notice how a tender touch increases your loving awareness.

This means having space for all the wildness, and choosing to hold it all with love. That’s the power of loving awareness.

Elaine Smookler is a Registered Psychotherapist (RP) and teacher and was a founding faculty member at the Centre for Mindfulness Studies in Toronto teaching clinical programs including MBCT and MBSR. She also taught Mindfulness throughout the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Medicine, was a founding teacher for the Mindfulness Thinktank at Sick Kids hospital and a longtime faculty member at the University of Toronto’s School of Continuing Studies where she taught her own program, “A Mindful Way through the Creative Process” and part of the certificate program, “Mindfulness Informed End-of-Life Care.”

Elaine has offered mindfulness training to every kind of participant including: parole Officers, the Catholic School Board, Summer Camp Owners, Hair Stylists, Children, Teens, Employee Assistance programs and a broad corporate audience. She is also a guide on the app “Dawn Personalized Cancer Stewardship Program.”

She has a focused psychotherapy practice offering clients support and precise tools to help them find the kindest, gentlest, most successful way forward to meet the difficulties, challenges and obstacles that life is constantly offering up. She also explores mindfulness themes as a key-note speaker, columnist, standup comedian, actor and singer. www.elainesmookler.com

Shlemiel the Painter Is Back: How Zig’s libc Rewrite Made SQLite Slower

📅 2026-10-26  |  Read Source →

Back in 2001, Joel Spolsky â whose writings had a big influence my career â wrote a great piece titled Back to Basics. The premise of the piece is that practitioners should understand the basics: However abstract and remote we may seem from the basic algorithms that drive computing, they can unexpectedly have enormous consequences on our projects.

One of his examples is the âShlemiel the Painterâ trap, where a seemingly simple choice leads to quadratic runtime complexity. In that parable, a street line painter never moves his can of paint. As he gets further and further along in the line, increasingly more of his time is spent walking to and from his can of paint.

It is astonishing how often this Shlemiel the Painter pattern recurs1, including now in 2026.

A few days ago I posted about a chess analysis service I put online â2. This is primarily a Rust service backed by sqlite that dishes out analysis tasks to runners. Each runner processes upwards of hundreds of chess games and return a large set of JSON bundles back to the main service, where they are processed and then stuffed into sqlite.

While the analysis pegs two dozen cores on a runner for minutes on end, the process of storing the data should take milliseconds. Sub-milliseconds.

Imagine my surprise when on the first really large set of games, the simple process of inserting the JSON data â maybe about 40,000 records â into the data store took minutes. During all of my testing this never really appeared as a critical path, but with a large set of records it suddenly was a breaking problem.

What made this more perplexing was that it completely saturated a core, being a CPU-bound operation. How could inserting simple JSON into SQLite yield minutes of CPU time?

Shlemiel the painter has made an appearance. To drop a spoiler, he was introduced to the project via Zigâs cc compiler and its replacement for standard library functions.

The project isnât built in Zig, but instead uses Rust. The sqlx sqlite crate needs to be compiled for the target environment â sqlite is of course a C project â so to facilitate cross-platform building, generating both Mac ARM64 and Linux ARM64 / x86-64 binaries from this machine in a convenient build and deploy workflow, zig cc is used to compile sqlite when targeting Linux, generously offering up cross-platform targeting via cargo-zigbuild.

From one build and deploy script on my Mac I can target all of my platforms without containers or build machines. Zigâs elegant libzigc re-implements the standard library so you can static link the necessary functionality.

Zig uses musl (the standard library rewrite), but they have been rewriting it piece by piece in pure Zig (via libzigc), removing the C dependencies one at a time.

And thatâs where the performance issue was introduced.

In the rewrite of strspn, replacing the musl version with the pure zig variant), the first step measures the entire length of the string. This is also seen in the rewrites of strcspn, strpbrk and strstr.

This is a problem for tokenizers. A tokenizer takes a giant string and a common iterating step is to skip whitespace, getting the new string location and then repeating this pattern repeatedly. With this shlemiel the painter pattern introduced with these rewrites, as it steps through the text it is tokenizing it is remeasuring the entire length of the string endlessly.

This is what caused my performance issue, and itâs why it appeared on Linux but was never seen on my Mac (where zig wasnât used for compiling sqlite).

Tokenizing a 1.2MB file, which was seen passing json to sqlite, is approximately 12,000x slower with this pattern. As the file gets larger, the slowdown is quadratic.

I mean no malice or disrespect to anyone involved with these great tools that enable so much. But itâs interesting that in the year 2026, these same old issues can recur, and we all need to be vigilant for them. Something so trivial was grinding a process to a halt, in the most unexpectedly trivial of places.

My original fix for this issue, at least in my own code, was to pre-prune whitespace from JSON, which greatly reduced the cost when tokenizing in sqlite3, but not knowing where else it might bite I moved my Linux builds over to Linux containers.

Years and years ago, back when Sunspider was the go-to benchmark and browsers would herald their supremacy, the same pattern could be seen in the way Firefox handled string concatenations, causing it to be a laggard in that benchmark. Sunspiderâs benchmark run somehow entailed an enormous number of string concatenations â even the tests having little to do with strings â and a simple profile3 of a benchmark run showed that a significant amount of the runtime was consumed constantly allocating slightly larger string memory, copying to the new location, and then repeating this pattern. It was Shlemiel the Painter.

I corrected this (overallocate strings with a size-dependent buffer such that subsequent concatenations could reuse the buffer until it actually need to be resized again, which again would overallocate), blogged about it, Brendon Eich took note, and voila Firefox took the lead in the benchmark4. Such a trivial thing turned it from slowpoke to benchmark. â©

Iâm under no delusions Iâm going to support my family with a niche chess analysis service, and at most Iâm looking to break even with the costs of running it. I put it online because I found my work to these ends useful to my own game, and hope that occasionally it will find the right user without burdening me with the costs of doing so. â©

Profilers are awesome. They are the most powerful tool we have available to us, so itâs strange to me how seldom they are utilized. â©

And for what itâs worth, string concatenation was extremely common in almost all web projects, so the benefit was substantial in the real world as well. There was a best practice of using string builders, but so often people just slammed strings together in a loop. â©

CSS-Tricks has a new owner!

📅 2026-10-26  |  Read Source →

This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news:

CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again!

Just to recap: DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022 from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase.

Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site.

So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have a small, awesome team to help with the day-to-day management of the site.

That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion.

Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while.

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone, no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right.

It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently.

In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots.

So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise, please do reach out!

Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners.

(And you can now support the site by becoming a member — thanks in advance!)

Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap.

And yes, I do believe that learning the basics is more important now than ever. But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are down across the board. It has to be done differently.

There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see.

Oh, and the newsletter. That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus.

That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going.

But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling.

That also means the guest writing form is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit.

I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can. Unless it’s a slop submission, of course.

Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight.

I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or helping with sponsorships. I gag at the thought of titles, but publisher hits best for me. My fingers are in all the bowls, but my most important responsibilities are:

The best thing I can possibly do is help folks develop a voice and give them a stage to use it. It’s about community and culture building. Publisher. That’s more my jam.

You totally can. I put a little membership deal together where you can join a members-only community on Discord along with some perks. Or check out the new shop. Or purchase advertising for your company. In the near-future you will be able to purchase the aforementioned course as well. Any little bit helps, of course. I squirm at the thought of asking for money, so there’s no pressure.

Support doesn’t even have to be financial! We all know that content publishers need all the eyeballs we can get in these prompt-filled days. Things like subscribing to the newsletter, sharing articles you like with others, clicking through from your RSS app, and checking out our sponsors are all very, very great ways to support us.

Yeah, me too. This post could go on and on. I’m an open book, though, and I’m happy to answer anything you might have in the comments. I know, so 2015, right?

Feyenoord preserved their four-point advantage over champions PSV after coming away with a point from Eindhoven thanks to an improved second-half performance.

PSV dominated the first half as they deployed a close-passing, tiki-taka style to stifle Feyenoord, but only had Guus Til’s well-taken volley after 20 minutes to show for it.

Ten minutes after the break Feyenoord equalised when Anis Hadj Moussa was given too much space to charge down the right flank and bend a shot inside the far post.

The Algerian had a good chance for a second towards the end, while PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovar had to be alert to keep out a header by Nacho Ferri from close range.

“We were by far the better team today and had the better chances,” said PSV coach Peter Bosz. “We started the second half badly and made a mistake, after which Hadj Moussa scored. And even then we could have won it.”

Ajax overtook PSV to close the gap at the top to three points with a hard-fought win at Sparta. Veteran striker Jens Toornstra scored for Sparta on his 500th Eredivisie appearance, but Abdellah Ouazane and Tolu Arokodare, the scorers against Atalanta in midweek, were on target again to claim the win for Ajax.

Twente moved up to fourth place as two late goals by Sondre Ørjasæter and Lucas Vennegoor of Hesselink earned a 2-0 win at AZ Alkmaar, who like Twente and PSV have 20 points.

Fortuna Sittard also snatched the points late on against Excelsior as Rodrigo Guth headed in a corner in injury time to keep the Limburg club in sixth place, two points further back.

At the other end of the table, the return of Adrie Koster as veteran coach brought no relief to Willem II, who crashed to a 6-1 home defeat to Cambuur.

The Tilburgers remain four points behind ADO Den Haag, who were unable to keep up the momentum of last week’s win against PSV as they lost 3-2 at home to Heerenveen.

Telstar lost by the same margin at Go Ahead Eagles, whose striker Søren Tengstedt netted twice in the first half to lead the Eredivisie scoring charts with eight goals.

AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)

📅 2026-10-26  |  Read Source →

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

Beware, A Disability Can Force You Into Early Retirement

📅 2026-10-26  |  Read Source →

Earlier this year, I was sick for two weeks. Unfortunately, I’ve had asthma since I was a kid. So when a respiratory illness hits, I tend to cough and suffer longer than the average person.

During COVID, my asthma flared up more often, likely due to the stress of having a baby during a pandemic.

It’s the type of breathing where you’re annoyingly conscious of every breath. You can never quite fill your lungs to 100%. In my case, it felt more like 75%.

On Wednesday, August 12, still sick, I decided to keep a previously scheduled consulting call with an FS reader. I had booked it assuming I’d be better by then. I wasn’t.

By the end of our 1 hour, 15 minute session, where I spent about 80% of the time talking, I was wiped out. My energy had dropped to maybe 30%. When you’re talking nonstop, you’re not breathing deeply or regularly. I felt like I was slowly suffocating while discussing their asset allocation.

The call reminded me of the many days I felt physically drained talking to clients during my 13 years in finance. As my responsibilities and stress grew, I eventually hit a breaking point. I’d rather earn nothing and be free and healthy than keep grinding myself down.

Just the other day, I couldn’t bend down to pick something up without a sharp pain shooting through my spine. I almost collapsed.

The last time I felt pain this bad was in 2023. I had spent an hour sitting on the ground signing copies of Buy This Not That for readers who donated to victims of the Maui fires. My dad is from Hawaii, and seeing thousands of lives upended overnight weighed on me. The Financial Samurai community ended up donating about $48,000. But when the signing was over, I couldn’t stand up and I called my wife for help.

My theory is that these episodes are triggered by a combination of prolonged stress and me forgetting I’m not 25 anymore.

This time, I clearly forgot. On Sunday, I played two hours of 4.5-level pickleball, then taught my kids for another hour. On Monday, I played 1.5 hours of intense tennis with plenty of serving. Then on Tuesday, several dads in our dad bod challenge shared their gym Personal Records, so naturally I went for personal records too. Instead of my usual three sets of 10-12 reps, I did five sets with progressive loading.

Wednesday morning, my back was already grumbling. So of course I went on a hilly 30-minute walk at 7:05am before breakfast and the school drop off. Walking downhill to school, the pain returned. By the time I got home, I could no longer walk normally.

If I still had a day job, there’s no way I could have gone into the office. And if my asthma flared up at the same time, I couldn’t speak to clients for more than an hour or two a day.

Not being able to provide for my family would be a terrible thing.

These two episodes forced me to confront a few uncomfortable truths:

Some people picture disability as a dramatic car accident or a fall off a ladder. Reality is far more boring. Accidental injuries make up only about 9% to 12% of long-term disability claims, while musculoskeletal problems like back and joint pain are the leading cause, at 26% to 33% of claims.

According to the Social Security Administration (SSA), roughly one in four 20-year-olds will be out of work for at least a year because of a disabling condition before reaching normal retirement age. That’s one quarter of all 20-year-olds, not just those in high-risk occupations.

In other words, the thing that takes you out of the workforce probably won’t be a skydiving mishap. It’ll be your back after one too many weightlifting attempts.

Before getting into what to do, it’s worth understanding the two main types of disability coverage. They work very differently.

Short-term disability (STD) covers you for a temporary inability to work, like recovering from surgery, a bad back, or a serious illness. Benefits typically replace around 50% to 70% of your income and last anywhere from a few weeks to about six months. The waiting period, called the elimination period, is usually short, often one to two weeks.

Many employers provide short-term disability as a benefit. A handful of states also run their own programs, including California (SDI), New York, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Hawaii (TDI). If you’re self-employed, you probably have nothing unless you bought it yourself.

Long-term disability (LTD) kicks in when a disability lasts longer, usually after a 90-day elimination period. It typically replaces about 60% of your income and can pay for a set number of years or until age 65. This is the coverage that actually protects your family’s financial future. Short-term disability is a speed bump. Long-term disability is a car crash.

And no, don’t count on Social Security Disability Insurance to save you. SSDI is hard to qualify for, has a five-month waiting period, and the monthly benefit is modest. It’s a floor, not a plan.

If you have a job with benefits, log into your HR portal today and look at your LTD coverage. Many group policies cap monthly benefits, which means high earners may only be replacing a fraction of their income.

If there’s a gap, buy a supplemental individual policy, ideally with an own-occupation rider. It’s portable, so it stays with you if you leave your job. If you’re self-employed like me, individual LTD is the only coverage you’ll have. Get quotes while you’re young and healthy, because pre-existing conditions get excluded or priced up later.

Even with great coverage, there’s a gap. Short-term disability might make you wait a week or two, and long-term disability usually makes you wait 90 days. Meanwhile, your mortgage, tuition, and Costco runs don’t pause.

Keep at least six months of living expenses in cash or Treasury bills. If you have kids, a single income household, or are self-employed, aim for 12 months. If you’re wondering where the line is between prudent and paranoid, here’s my take on how much savings is too much. The emergency fund is your bridge from healthy to covered.

A single income stream is a single point of failure. If that engine stalls, the whole plane goes down. Your goal is to build a jet with at least four engines, so you can lose one and still land safely.

The best time to start a side hustle is while you still have a steady paycheck and good health. You get to experiment without pressure, and if it fails, you still eat.

I started Financial Samurai in July 2009 while working full-time in finance. I’d wake up early and write before work, then publish again on weekends. For three years, it made very little money. But by the time I left Corporate America in 2012, the site had become a real second engine alongside about $80,000 a year in passive investment income.

Without that second engine, I never would have had the courage to negotiate my way out.

Here’s the key for disability planning: prioritize side hustles that don’t require your body to show up. Driving for Uber or coaching tennis stops the moment your back gives out. Writing, a blog, a YouTube channel, an online course, or a self-published ebook can keep paying while you’re flat on your back.

If you need ideas, my wife put together a list of the 20 best side hustle ideas to make extra money. If you want to go the online route, here’s how to start a blog and build your own platform. I’m biased, but owning your own corner of the internet is the gift that keeps on giving.

One engine is a job. Two engines is a cushion. Four or more engines is freedom.

Your peak earning years are also, conveniently, your peak health years. Don’t assume your income will keep climbing forever. Assume it could drop to zero tomorrow, then save as if that’s true.

Related: Achieving FI With A Visual Impairment

I saved over 50% of my after-tax income starting with my first job out of college because I knew I couldn’t last a lifetime working 70+ hours a week. I didn’t know my lungs and back would eventually join the protest, but the logic held up.

Front-load your savings. Max out your 401(k) and IRA, and invest the excess in a taxable brokerage account. Pay down high fixed costs where you can.

The lower your required monthly expenses, the less income replacement you need if disaster strikes. A paid-off house is one of the best disability insurance policy nobody talks about.

Your ability to earn over the next 20 to 30 years is likely worth millions. Yet we manage our portfolios more carefully than our bodies.

Get annual checkups. But lock down a life insurance policy before you see a doctor for something more. Manage your stress before it manages you. Warm up, cool down, and stop trying to beat the other dads’ PRs after a weekend of nonstop racquet sports. Ask me how I know.

While you’re at it, get your paperwork in order. A will, a durable power of attorney, and a healthcare directive are the basics. But if anyone depends on your income, term life insurance is the most important piece. A disability takes away your ability to earn for a while. Death takes it away for good.

The irony is that the health problems that make you worry about disability also make life insurance more expensive, or harder to get. Lock in coverage while you’re still healthy enough to qualify. I’d compare term life quotes on Policygenius, which lets you see prices from multiple top insurers in one place.

The scary thing about disability is that it rarely announces itself. One day you’re serving aces and going for gym PRs. The next, you can’t walk your kids to school.

Being unable to breathe normally or walk for a few days made me realize how fragile everything is. If you’re the provider for your family, that fragility is your responsibility to plan for.

So check your disability coverage this week. Build your cash buffer. Start a side hustle that doesn’t depend on your body showing up. And for goodness sake, stretch.

Have you ever been unable to work for an extended period due to an illness or injury? Do you know whether your employer’s long-term disability policy is own-occupation or any-occupation, and when it switches? How many engines of income do you have today, and which would keep running if you couldn’t get out of bed? Have you bought supplemental disability insurance, or do you think it’s a waste of money? And what side hustle would you start if your main income disappeared tomorrow?

This post is about how quickly your ability to earn can disappear. The best defense is building wealth and multiple income streams during your healthiest years, before your back and lungs start filing complaints.

That’s exactly what I lay out in my USA Today bestseller, Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures. I’ve distilled 30 years of experience studying, working in, and writing about personal finance into a roadmap for reaching $1 million and beyond, while you still have the energy to enjoy it.

Get a copy today. Your future self, possibly lying flat on the floor with a bad back, will thank you.

The own-occupation versus any-occupation distinction was the part that stood out most to me, since a policy that only pays when you cannot do any job is far weaker than it first sounds. I had a concussion which another cyclist collided into me over a decade ago. I was 54 yrs. I lost my memory for 4 hrs. and have no memory of people helping to get off bike path, transported by ambulance to hospital, etc. It was like the movies…I woke up in pain and was on a spinal bord in ICU ward, with my partner and neurology dr. bending over, testing my memory after I awoke. I had to learn to walk slowly in lst few wks., I was dizzy just standing in the shower or in front of my kitchen sink, turning. I had to rest for many hours in bed for well over a month. If I walked too fast, I got dizzy from seeing blur of colours of scenery around me, etc. Thankfully as part of employer’s benefit, I had short-term disability insurance which I had to tap into long-term disability insurance. I returned to work lst part-time after 5 months on disability /medical leave. I returned to cycling slowly at 6 months. My partner did all the housework, cooking and food shopping during my recovery. It took me another few additional months to become comfortable even having other cyclists cycle around me.

It scared the beejesus out of me, because I solo paying off my home mortgage. My partner was still paying off his. This is what happens when you are solely responsible for your own mortgage or any huge loan/debt. Your financial vulnerability becomes even more acutely real. Thankfully at that time, I had a reverse mortgage.

I so strongly recommend any worker get disability insurance..and if you don’t have children, you don’t have to worry about life insurance. There’s far greater likelihood during your working years, you will not prematurely die young but more likely to have major injury/ surgery (broken leg, hip replacement, etc.) that will sideline you from your job for a few months or a yr. All of us, even the most healthy (like myself) will experience a major injury/illness where we can’t do our money-earning job.

I’m glad you are now OK and had insurance when that accident happened!

Sam, this article really hit home for me. At age 55, I began experiencing symptoms of an extremely rare disease. After years of uncertainty, dozens of doctors, and losing nearly 40 pounds, I suffered a stroke at 57 that abruptly ended my career in construction management and real estate development. Fortunately, the stroke spared my speech, cognition, and memory, but permanently impaired my left-side motor control and sensation. Thirteen years later, chronic pain, spasticity, and mobility limitations remain daily challenges. One lesson I’d emphasize is the importance of good health insurance. Medical bills totaled approximately $675,000 over four years, including $485,000 leading up to and including the stroke. Even with insurance, some rehabilitation required appeals or out-of-pocket payments. My stroke also forced me to sell my interest in our development business to my longtime partner. Although we had planned for a buyout in the event of death, disability was a different matter, and we ultimately negotiated an amicable agreement. I was fortunate to have accumulated substantial savings and investments before becoming disabled. Equally important, I was blessed with supportive family and friends, including a sister who’s a professional financial advisor, a physician brother-in-law, a daughter who’s an ER nurse, and a son who’s a mental health therapist. Unable to return to work, I focused more on managing our investments. With my sister’s guidance, we maintained a buy-and-hold approach through major market downturns. I’m a testament to time in the market, not timing the market, and the power of compounding. Our net worth has more than tripled since before the stroke. Meanwhile, rehabilitation remains a lifelong project. Now 71, I recently returned to my longtime neurological physical therapist after a three-year break. I’m still looking for ways to improve my independence, mobility, and quality of life. Forced retirement at 57 certainly didn’t mean the end of a productive and purposeful life. Financial independence can’t restore your health, but it provides options when life changes unexpectedly. My advice: Save and invest early, maintain good insurance, appreciate your support network, and don’t postpone enjoying life while you’re healthy.

Thank you for sharing your experience. It really hits Home, the importance of good health, good health insurance, and spending more intentionally with our one and only lives.

I wish you good health and prosperity. Don’t be a stranger!
